content.text: Swift provides us with a shortcut when using optionals: if you want to access something like `a.b.c` and `b` is optional, you can write a question mark after it to enable *optional chaining*: `a.b?.c`.

When that code is run, Swift will check whether `b` has a value, and if it’s `nil` the rest of the line will be ignored – Swift will return `nil` immediately. But if it *has* a value, it will be unwrapped and execution will continue.
To try this out, here’s an array of names:

We’re going to use the `first` property of that array, which will return the first name if there is one or `nil` if the array is empty. We can then call `uppercased()` on the result to make it an uppercase string:
That question mark is optional chaining – if `first` returns `nil` then Swift won’t try to uppercase it, and will set `beatle` to `nil` immediately.

title: Optional chaining
postscript: You can chain as many things as you need. For example, `someOptionalArray?.first?.lowercased()`.
question: This code is valid Swift – true or false?
hint: It might sound obvious, but optional chaining may only be used with optionals.

correct.answer:
let shoppingList = ["eggs", "tomatoes", "grapes"]
let firstItem = shoppingList.first?.appending(" are on my shopping list")

wrong.reason: The `loadForecast()` function does not return an optional string.
The `captains` array is optional, so this should read `captains?.last?.count`. Also, the array should not end with a question mark.
Accessing the `first` property returns an optional, so this should read `credentials.first?.lowercased()`.
Accessing a dictionary key is optional, so this should read `opposites["light"]?.uppercased()`.
The `count` property is not optional, so this should read `names.last?.count`.
The `attendees` array is not optional, so this should read `attendees.first?.uppercased`.
